caseno: Appellant from Appellate Decree No. 920 of 1966.
lawyer:
Moinul Huq ------ For the Appellant.
Ahmed Sobhan with A.T. Chowdhury ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Sona Mia & others ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Momraj Bhuiya & others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J-This appeal is directed against a judgment of affirmance decreeing a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession.

2. The plaintiffs have brought this suit on the allegation that the disputed lands, as described in schedule.1 to the plaint, originally belonged to Abdul Aziz alias Lal Miah and his five brothers who had rayati interest in the suit lands and used to cultivate the same through bargadars. At the time of the C.S. operation; Ramjan Ali and Kader Haji were bargadars in respect of the said lands and they were recorded as such in the C.S. Khatian. About a year after the Settlement Operation, the said bargadars gave up possession to the owners who, after cultivating the lands in Khas for some time, transferred these lands by 3 registered kabalas in 1923 and 1924, and one patta in 1935, to the predecessors of the plaintiffs. After acquiring these lands in the aforesaid manner; the plaintiff’s had been possessing the same till 1958 when the defendants forcibly disposed them from the land described in Schedule 11 to the plaint. Thereafter the suit was instituted on 18.12.1950 for declaration of title and recover of possession.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1 who filed a written statement contending inter alia that Ramjan Ali and Kader Haji the predecessors of the defendant had occupancy raryati right in the disputed lands and they had been recorded as such in the C.S. Katian. They denied that they were mere bargadars and had no tenancy right and that they did give up possession of the lands to Lal Mia and his brothers.

4. Both the Courts below held that Ramjan Ali and kader Haji who had been recorded a well as occupancy raiyats in respect of the disputed land had no right of tenancy therein and that the plaintiff’s had been in possession of the disputed land on the basis of title acquired by their predecessors by means of purchase and settlement and they had been dispossessed by the principal defendants from the said land.

5. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellants, contends that the judgment is bad in law because the Courts below have failed to attach any presumptive value to the record-of-rights which shows that the plaintiff’s predecessors had occupancy right in respect of the disputed lands and that there is no proper finding as to the date of dispossession being within 12 years from the date of institution of the suit. The learned Advocate has further contended that the recitals in deeds, Exts. 1 series and Ext. 2 are not admissible in evidence against the defendants for the purpose of disproving the defendant’s right of tenancy.

6. Mr. Ahmad Sobhan, on the other hand, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff, respondents, submits that the Courts below were correct in holding that the entries in the record of rights showing that the defendant’s predecessors were bargadars as well said records did not raise any presumption in favour of the defendant’s. Secondly, even if there was any such presumption, that has been sufficiently rebutted by the documentary and oral evidence that has been adduced in this case. Thirdly, Mr. Sobhan contends, even if the position that the defendant’s predecessors had the right of tenancy in respect of the disputed land is accepted to be true; the evidence of possession which has been brought on record in this case is sufficient to show that the plaintiff’s had been in possession of the disputed land for more than 12 years and as such any right which might have been acquired by them has been determined by such long possession.

7. The relevant records-of-right relate to khatian No. 80 and khatian No. 83 of Mouza Galim Khan which have been marked as Ext. 3 and Ext. A respectively Ext. 3 being in respect of khattan 80 of Mouza Galim khan purports to record the superior interest whereas Ext. A. which is in respect of khatian 83, purports to record in interest subordinate to khatian 80. In khatian 83, subordinate to khatian 80. In khatian Kader Haji have been recorded as বর্গা রায়ত স্থিতিবান in the column for the class of interest and in the column of rent, it is recorded “শয্যের জর্দ্ধেক” in the column of superior “খাজনা শামিল” and in the column of superior interest. “খতিয়ান ৮০ আবদুল আজিজ গং” In khatian 80, i. e. Ext. 3 Abdul Aziz and his 5 brothers have been recorded a owners but there is no entry to indicate their status, that is to say, whether they were raiyats or tenure holders and in the column for subordinate interest, khatian 81-84 have been mentioned. Exts. 1 to 1 (b) are three kabalas executed by Abdul Aziz and others, the recorded owners in Ext. 3 in favour of the predecessors of the present plaintiffs and Ext. 2 has been described as a “বেমেয়াদি রায়তি পাট্র।” executed by the same recorded owners in favour of the predecessors of the present plaintiffs. While considering the records-or-rights, both the Courts below have taken the view that the entries in Ext. A showing the predecessors of the defendants as raiyats as ewll as bargadars are inconsistent and, therefore, such entries cannot raise any presumption in favour of the right of tenancy of the defendants predecessors. It seems to us that both the Courts below have failed to show proper appreciation of the claim of tenancy by a person who used to cultivate lands under the system known as barga. Although this question has been the subject for judicial exposition on several previous occasions, it appears to us that none of the Courts below have properly grasped the legal character of the relationship peculiar to such a system Both the Courts below appear to have proceeded on the view that a bargadar, that is a person cultivating certain land under the system known as barga cannot be a tenant as such, although he may claim or acquire such status under certain circumstances after abandoning his character of a bargadar. They have, therefore, thought that the entries in the record-of-rights showing an occupier of land to be a bargadar as well as a tenant are inconsistent and no legal presumption can be attached to such entries. They have in a similar way, taken the view that when the defendants stated that they were bargadars under the plaintiffs or their predecessors, it was an admission on their predecessors; it was an admission on their part that they have had no right of tenancy.

<u>8. It has not been defined anywhere what a bargadar is we find in Wilson’s Glossaries, that the term barga has been defined as an agreement by which the cultivator engages to pay the landlord half of the produce, the latter providing half of the seed and paying the whole of the rent. From the definition of tenant as given in section 3, clause (17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act as it stood before the amendment of 1929, we find that a tenant means a person who holds land under another person and is or but for a special contract, would be liable to payment for that land to that person and in clause (13) of the same section, rent, has been defined as whatever is lawfully payable or deliverable in money or kind by a tenant to his landlord on account of the use or occupation of the land held by the tenant. So, we find that there is nothing in clause (13) or clause (17) of section 3 which militates against a bargadar being a tenant. Rent according to clause (13) of section 3, as we have seen, may be in money or in kind and it need not be a fixed amount, there is nothing in law to prevent a landlord from accepting a variable or fluctuating quantity of the produce of land as rent. Therefore, according to the provisions of law as were in force before 1929 there was nothing inherently inconsistent between the characters of a bargader and a tenant. Whether a bargadar has the character of a tenant or not depends upon the nature of the engagement between the landlord, i.e, the owner of the land and the bargadar who agrees to cultivate the lands on condition of delivering certain share of the produce of the land. If the intention of the parties is that a certain interest in land is to be demised by the transaction in question, then a right of tenancy will be created. But if, on the other hand, the intension is that the person who engages to cultivate the land would not acquire any interest in the land and would only cultivate it on the basis of certain remuneration which will be a share of the produce of the land then there will be no tenancy created in favour of the person. In one case, the intension of the parties is that there will be created an interest in favour of the occupier in respect of the land he cultivates and the owner of the land will receive a share of the produce by way of rent and in the other case no interest at all will be created in favour of the person cultivating the land, but he will receive a share of the crops grown by him by way of remuneration for the labour that he would devote for the cultivation of the land and growing the crops. So, it would always depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case whether a tenancy has been created or of a person on condition that he would cultivate it and give a certain share of the produce to the landlord. It was only in 1929 when by an amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the Legislature sought to bring about a certain change in regard to presumption about the status of a person who used to cultivate lands under barga system, by adding a proviso to the definition of “tenant” to section 3(17) of B.T. Act, which is to the following effect:</u>

<u>"Provided that a person who, under the system generally known as, adhi, barga or bhag cultivates the land of another person on condition of delivering a share of the produce to that person, is not a tenant, unless-</u>

<u>(ii) such person has been expressly admitted to be a tenant by his landlord in any document executed by him or executed in his favour and accepted by him, or</u>

<u>(ii) He has been or is held by a Civil Court to be a tenant."</u>

9. The legal implication of this proviso has been considered in a number of cases, more important of which may be noticed here. A Single Judge of the Dacca High Court (Hamoodur Rahman, J), as the learned Judge then was took the view on an interpretation of the proviso to section 3 (17) of the B T. Act, in the case of Abu Naser Sayedullah Vs Abdul Malik, reported in 12 DLR 206 same case PLD 1960 Dacca 587, that a bargadar was not nettled to put up a defence of his tenancy, in a suit for recovery of money on account of non-delivery of barga produce in respect of a period subsequent to the introduction of the Amending Act of 1929. Reliance was placed by the learned Single Judge on a decision of the Calcutta High Court reported as Sishumohan Koyal and others Vs. Rajendra Nath Sarcar and others In AIR 1938 Cal. 707.

10. Subsequently a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court (Hasan and Idris, JJ.) in the case of Kumir Mondal and others Vs Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and others reported in 14 DLR 810 same case as PLD 1963 Dacca 886, took a different view as to the interpretation of the aforesaid proviso over-ruling the decision in the case of Abu Naser Sayedullah and Hasan J. in delivering the judgment in the said case, observed as follows:—

"The words’s held by a Civil Court', are clear enough to show that though the bargadar was not recognized expressly as a tenant by the landlord and has not been already held by the Civil Court as a tenant, yet the Court can take into consideration the evidence and circumstances in the case and come to a finding that a bargadar is a tenant. So the words 'is held by the Civil Court' do not debar a Civil Court to find the defendant bargadar as a tenant and those words are also a pointer that a bargadar is not debarred from pleading that he is a tenant for a period subsequent to the introduction of the proviso as held in the case of Abu Naser Sayedullah Vs Abdul Malik alias Malo and the case of Sishu Mahan Kayal and others Vs. Rajendra Nath Sarkar and others 1 hold that the proviso is neither retrospective nor does it debar the bargadar to plead that he is a tenant, but only has laid down certain rules for determination of the status".

11. On an appeal the Supreme Court of Pakistan affirmed the decision of the Division Bench, in the case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and others Vs. Kumir Mondal and others reported in 19 DLR (SC) 392 same case PLD 1965 (S.C.) 434, although it thought that the endeavor of the learned Judges of the High Court to discover the Legislative intent as to whether the proviso was retrospective or prospective was an unnecessary academic exercise, Hamoodur Rahman, J. in delivering the judgment of the Supreme Court, observed as follows:

“It seems to us that the only change that the Legislature has laboured to bring about is to lay down that only in the first instance there will be a presumption that a person holding under a system of barga or bhag is not a tenant, but this presumption will be rebutted only if it is  established that he has been admitted by the landlord to be a tenant or is declared in a previous suit to be a tenant or if he can in a suit where this question is put in issue establish his status as such tenant. In effect, it seems that the Legislature has laboured in vain or worse, avoided its responsibility and really thrown the burden upon the Court to resolve this question, for; the net result appears in substance, to be to leave the question where it was, apart from shifting the burden of proof on the tenant. To this extent possibly there has been a departure from the old principle."

12. As it has been pointed out by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that, even after the said amendment if a bargadar or adhiar or bhagdar has not been admitted as a tenant by a landlord nor has been adjudged a tenant by a Civil Court he can still raise a contention in any suit that he is a tenant and such a contention shall have to be decided on the basis of the evidence that may he adduced in that case It will appear from the judgment of the learned District Judge as well as from that of the learned Subordinate Judge who tried that quit, that they proceeded on the view that the term bargadar itself is a negation of the right of tenancy. The learned District Judge, at page 21 of the paper book after referring to the entries in Ext. A observed;

"Different interpretations have been given to the meaning of these two peculiar entries which appear to be inconsistent. According to the plaintiffs Lal Mia and his brothers who were themselves occupancy ramjets could not have created another occupancy raiyati under them and that, in fact, they were the actual raiyati and under them Ramjan Ali and Kader Haji were mere bargadar giving half of the crops as barga which might have been wrongly stated as ‘খাজনা’or rent."

13. The learned District Judge seems to be of the view that there cannot be one occupancy right under another occupancy right and that these entries which have recorded barga as well as রায়ত স্থিতিবান are inconsistent, and makes further observation in the following manner at page 28 of the paper book:—

"Entry in the Khatian to the effect that Ramjan Ali and Kader Haji had occupancy rights রায়ত স্থিতিবান got no basis Secondly, on the very face of it, it is being inconsistent in respect of these two matters barga and occupancy rights. No legal presumption can be attached to such a Khatian containing incorrect and inconsistent statements."

<u>14. Apart from the question that it conceivable in law to have an occupancy right under another occupancy raiyat, although the status of the subordinate tenant will be that of an under rayiat, the learned District Judge seems to have made a mistake of fact in taking the view that the entries have no value because they purport to record one occupancy right under another occupancy right. This is not correct so far as the entries are concerned. As it will appear from Ext. 3 which is the superior khatian the record and owners have not been recorded as occupancy radials. It has been pointed out earlier, that there has been no entry in the column of 'Class of interest of the occupier' in the said khatian. Therefore, the ground which has weighed with the learned District Judge in inducing him to take the view that the defendants cannot claim to the right of tenancy because of the entries showing one occupancy right under another occupancy right has no basis.</u>

15. The learned District Judge seems to have proceeded on the wrong view that the term bargadar is an antithesis of the term 'tenant' and that a person so long as he is a bargadar cannot claim a right of tenancy. The learned District Judge while assessing the evidence on record has therefore taken the view that when the defence witnesses have stated that the defendants were bargadars or that they delivered half of the crops to the plaintiffs or to plaintiffs predecessors, they have admitted that they had no right of tenancy, The learned District Jude, it appears to us was clearly in error in regard to his aforesaid approach to the evidence on record, and his endings have been vitiated as a result of want of proper appreciation of the real nature of the question involved. It may be pointed out that the same mistake was committed by the trial Court we are of the opinion that the judgment under appeal cannot be sustained.

16. Mr. Moinul Huq has also submitted that the Courts below have laid undue mess upon the recitals of Ext. 1 series, which, according to him, are not at all admissible against the contesting defendants of these documents Exts. 1 to 1 (b) and Ext. 2 are the documents of title of the plaintiffs. Ext. 1 (c) is a deed of transfer in favour of a third person in respect of the land of same khatian, and Exts. 1 (d) and 1 (e) are deeds of transfer in favour of the predecessors of the defendants in respect of the land of the same khatian. It is contended on behalf of the respondents that in these documents it has been clearly asserted that the recorded owners arc the owners in possession of these lands and the recitals disprove the claim of tenancy by the appellants. The Courts below proceeded also in the view that there are clear statements in these documents which belie the defence case. It may be pointed out that what has been asserted in all these documents is that the vendors or the executants having had raiyati right in the lands coveted by the respective transactions were owners in possession and for the facility of cultivation or management they were making the transfers. Strictly speaking the Courts below were not correct in their view that there was an assertion of occupancy right of khas possession in these documents.

17. Mr. Moinul Huq submits that these recitals are not admissible against his clients under section 13(a) of the Evidence Act because these statements were not asserted by the transactions in question although they may be assertions in the said transactions and in support of his contention he has referred to the case of Ronald Duncan Cromartic and Francis Arthur Shephard  Sutherland Vs. Sri Sri Iswar Radha Damodar Jew reported in 62 Calcutta Law Journal at page 10, in which it was held that an assertion in a mortgage deed that the properties were secular properties were admissible in evidence under section 13 of the Evidence Act, but as against the plaintiffs the evidentiary value was very slight. The next case referred to by him was the case of Brojendra Kishore Roy Chowdhury Vs. Mohim Chandra Bhattacharji & others reported in 31 Calcutta Weekly Note page 32 same case AIR 927 Cal Page 1 in which it was held that mere assertion of a right in a document, to which the person against whom the right was asserted was not a party and of which he knew nothing was not to “claim a right” within the meaning of section 13(a) of the Evidence Act. In this case, the view expressed by Mukerji, J and endorsed by the Bench constituted by the Bench constituted by 3 others and presided over by Sanderson, Chief Justice was to the effect that a transaction within the meaning of section 13 of the Evidence Act was one by which the vendor asserted his competency to transfer the property, that is to say that he had such interest in the property as would enable him to undertake the transaction but the other statement, i.e. whether the right claimed by him was a nishkar or not was not an assertion by the transaction within the meaning of the said section. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate was the case reported in Kanta Mohan Mallik and others Vs. Basudeb Ghora and others reported in 39 Calcutta Weekly Notes Page 30 which relying upon the case reported in 31 Calcutta Weekly Notes page 32, held that a kabala in which it was asserted that the vendor had nishkar right in the property which was a subject matter of the sale was not admissible in evidence for the purpose of proving nishkar. In this connection, the other cases which are appropriate for the purpose viz AIR 1932 Calcutta page 427 and AIR 1947 Calcutta page 209, may also be referred to.

18. It is to be pointed out that the plaintiffs case is that the plaintiffs predecessors had occupancy raiyati right in the disputed lands which they used to possess in khas and they had no subordinate tenants under them in respect of the suit lands, whereas the substantive defence case is that it was the defendant’s predecessors who, though bargadars had occupancy raiyati right in the said lands and had been possessing the same as such and the plaintiff’s predecessors were in the position of landlords realising barga produce the said lands. If the sale deeds, Ext 1 series and the patta Ext. 2 can be construed to mean that right of khas possession was sought to be transferred by the said deeds, then it can be reasonably contended that this right of khas possession was asserted by the plaintiffs predecessors by the said transaction, and they purpose of supporting the plaintiff’s case and disproving the defendants contention. The sale deeds Exts; 1(d) and 1(e), which are in not ipso facto demolish the defendants case, as had been supported by the Courts below and also strenuously argued by Mr Sobhan, the learned Advocate for the respondents. There is no incongruity between the existence of tenancy right of the defendants predecessors and their purchase of the superior right so as to absolve themselves from the obligation of payment of barga rent. If, however, the said documents, viz Exts 1(d) and 1(e) can be construed as asserting khas possession of the plaintiffs predecessors in the disputed khatian and transferring the same to the defendants predecessors, they will certainly be admissible in evidence in support of the plaintiffs case, as had been mentioned above, for the purpose of rebutting the presumption created by the C.S. record-of-rights. We, therefore, do not accept the contention of Mr. Moinul Huq that these documents are not admissible in evidence at all.

19. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, has contended that the documentary evidence which has been adduced is sufficient to rebute the presumption if any, which may have been raised by the record-of-rights, Ext. A. as most of the documentary evidence are more than 30 years old and in this connection he has referred to the case reported in (1878) 3 Appeal Cases 644, pages 667 and 668 and (1899) 2 Chancery Division page 81. It may be ported but however, that both the Courts below have misconceived the character of the interest as evidenced by the entries in the record-or-rights and, as such, failed to consider the evidence from the correct standpoint. Because of this defect in the initial approach, the findings which have been arrived at, are not sustainable at all. The documents which have been proved by the plaintiff if they do actually prove the assertion or claim that the plaintiff had been possessing the lands in khas and that the defendants had no right of tenancy in the disputed land.

<u>20. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan has drawn our attention to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case reported in 17 DLR (Supreme Court) 392 (which has already been referred to in another connection ) as to the presumption of correctness of a record-of-rights. It has been held in the said decision that the presumption of correctness of the record-of-rights if applicable only to the state of things as were existing at the time when the records were prepared, the further presumption that the same state of things has continued is under section 114 of the Evidence Act and the presumption of correctness of the record-of-rights weakens with the passage of time. It is true that in determining the question whether the defendants have got the tenancy right in the same may as their predecessors had, as recorded in the record-of-rights in the year, 1919, is based upon the second kind of presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act. But a Court of facts shall have to consider that, if the entry in the record-of-rights that the predecessors of the present defendants had tenancy right is presumed to have been correct at the time when the records were prepared, then the Court is also to satisfy itself that the said state of things was brought to an end in course of time by some other act or event. Therefore, in any view of matter, the evidence on record will have to be re-assessed attaching the necessary presumptive value to the said record or rights.</u>

21. Having regard to the erroneous approach of the Courts below in respect of the evidence on record we find however that there is substance in the contention of Mr. Moinul Huq that there is no proper finding as to whether the plaintiffs had possession in the disputed land within 12 years from the date of the suit. There should be a proper finding on this question as well on the evidence adduced in the case.

22. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan has also submitted that, since the evidence on record is sufficient, this Court instead of sending the case on remand to the lower Court may bear the case on the basis of the evidence and decide it once and for all. It has also been submitted in this connection that, if necessary this Court can keeps the appeal pending and send for a necessary decision on any matter under the provisions of Order 41, rule 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

23. Since the case is a very old one being instituted in the year 1959, we have given anxious thought to these submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants, but having regard to the fact that both the Courts of facts having misconceived the legal aspect of the question involved and having failed to assess the evidence from the correct stand-point we are of the opinion that it is better that the evidence should he re-assessed by the last Court of facts, viz., the lower appellate Court and come to the necessary finding on the question involved.

We, therefore, allow this appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below and remand the case to the Court of the District Judge for rehearing of the appeal. It has already been pointed out that the case is a very old one and, as such, the hearing of appeal should be taken up within two months from the date of arrival of the records in the Court below. The records of the case should he expeditiously sent down.

The cost of the appeal will abide the result.

M. N. Huda, J.—I agree.

End.
